title: SYSK Selects: How Grief Works
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the April 2011-era episode "How Grief Works" (the host intro says "April of two thirt," a transcription artifact). Josh and Chuck explore grief as a personal, non-linear experience. They cover animal grief (Domini the elephant at the Prince of Wales Zoo in Lucknow, India, and the debate over whether animals truly grieve), types of grief (anticipatory, unanticipated, ambiguous), Elisabeth Kübler-Ross's five stages (denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance) and the critique that they are not a fixed sequence, recent widow/widower studies on duration and variability, the DSM-5 proposal to remove the bereavement exclusion for depression, coping advice (avoid drugs and alcohol, memorial projects, honoring the deceased through causes), complicated grief and its risk factors, pet loss, and Victorian mourning customs and post-mortem photography. The episode ends with administrative details thanking listeners for gifts and mail.

segments.title: Selects intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces this SYSK Selects pick, How Grief Works, and the hosts joke about the phrase 'good grief' and minced oaths.

segments.title: Elephant Domini and animal grief
segments.summary: Josh recounts how Domini, a 72-year-old elephant at the Prince of Wales Zoo in Lucknow, India, grieved the death of her younger pregnant friend Chumpacali, who died in childbirth with a stillborn calf. Domini stopped eating and drinking and died days later. The hosts discuss scientists divided over whether animals truly grieve, including the chimpanzee carrying her dead baby.

segments.title: Grief is personal; types of grief
segments.summary: The hosts say grief is highly personal and that psychology has not fully defined it. They describe anticipatory grief, unanticipated grief (such as a sudden accidental death), and ambiguous grief (such as a disappearance or abandonment), and note grief need not come only from death.

segments.title: Kübler-Ross's five stages of grief
segments.summary: The hosts explain Elisabeth Kübler-Ross's 1969 five stages (denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance) and criticize treating them as a fixed sequence. They discuss a W-shaped chart of the stages and recent widow and widower studies showing day-to-day oscillation and recovery over roughly six months to three years.

segments.title: Depression, DSM-5 and medicalizing grief
segments.summary: The hosts discuss depression as a stage of grief and how it differs from a recognized mental disorder. They cover the proposed DSM-5 change removing the bereavement exclusion, which they say could medicalize grief.

segments.title: Coping with grief
segments.summary: The hosts discuss healthy coping: avoiding drugs and alcohol, eating right and exercising, writing letters to the deceased, making memorials or memory videos, and channeling grief into projects or causes the deceased would have cared about, such as Mothers Against Drunk Driving.

segments.title: Studies on grief prevalence and relief
segments.summary: The hosts summarize studies finding that significant grief is a minority experience among bereaved people, that therapy is not helpful for everyone, and that some people who were unhappy in their marriages feel relief after a spouse dies. They say a lack of visible grief does not mean something is wrong, and that men and women may grieve differently.

segments.title: Complicated grief and trauma
segments.summary: The hosts describe complicated grief, in which daily life is disrupted for months, and note risk factors such as the death of a child, sudden or traumatic death, or a very close dependent relationship. They distinguish grief from trauma, noting traumatic dreams about oneself being endangered.

segments.title: Pet loss
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how losing a pet can be as painful as losing a person for some people, and advise talking with others who understand and not feeling embarrassed about grieving a pet.

segments.title: Victorian mourning and post-mortem photography
segments.summary: The hosts describe Paul Rosenblatt's study of fifty-six Victorian diaries, in which mourners tried to keep the deceased present and carried grief for life. They mention Victorian black mourning dress and bereavement photography, and a listener email about hand and foot casts given by a hospital after a child's death.

segments.title: Sign-off and administrative details
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode, point listeners to howstuffworks.com for more on grief, and read thank-you notes for listener gifts and mail.
